patch_entries.tldr: A 10–13 µGal gravity pulse at the eclipse contacts is exactly what WIN-011 already claims, restated with a future eclipse window. The supporting Mohe 1997 data predates this April-2026 registration by 29 years, and four superconducting gravimeters (Van Camp et al. 2001) found no eclipse gravity signal — so wrapping the old claim in a future date adds no new predictive content.

Predicts the North Magnetic Pole will reach 141–146°E by 2031 — an extrapolation IGRF/WMM already publish from the same NOAA pole-trajectory data. The dome adds no derivation: if the pole arrives in that band, standard geomagnetism gets the credit; if it does not, both models miss together.

Predicts the NMP drift ratio stays ≥2.0× through 2028, which is just WIN-043 (already verdicted Std Model Explains) extended forward. The ratio is arithmetic from published NOAA pole positions — confirming it does not distinguish dome geometry from standard geomagnetism.

Schumann resonance shifts upward when solar wind compresses the ionosphere — that is textbook magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling, not a dome prediction. The ≥7.85 Hz threshold during >5 nPa solar wind sits inside the normal 7.7–8.0 Hz diurnal band, and the underlying data predates registration.

NMP poleward-vs-equatorward dominance is fully explained by core-mantle boundary flux dynamics in standard geophysics, and the author has self-marked this REFINED because lateral drift actually dominates. The pole trajectory itself is already covered by WIN-043 (Std Model Explains); registering it again adds no new test.

The dome predicted Polaris elevation would systematically exceed WGS84-predicted latitude above 55°N; the author has self-classified this as FALSIFIED. WIN-065 already documents that the +0.27° excess at 35.9°N sits within the known 0.74° refraction/instrument offset, so the dome-side prediction collapses on its own scoresheet.
